items.title: SUB-SURFACE VENTURI KINETIC HARVESTING (SVKH): A ZERO-PROFILE IN-GROUND AERODYNAMIC FRAMEWORK FOR EXTREME CYCLONIC WINDS AND PASSIVE INERTIAL SAND SEPARATION IN HYPER-ARID METROPOLITAN ENVIRONMENTS
items.abstract: Conventional horizontal axis wind turbines must cease generating precisely when atmospheric kinetic energy peaks: above a cut out speed near 25 m/s, the tower overturning moment M = F·h and blade fatigue loading force emergency braking, so a storm whose energy flux scales as v³ yields no wind power to the city it threatens. In the hyper arid, coastal Arabian Peninsula the paradox is aggravated by Shamal windstorms, convective downbursts and intensifying Arabian Sea cyclones, all of which carry abrasive silica particulate that scours blades and seizes bearings. This paper introduces the Sub-Surface Venturi Kinetic Harvester (SVKH), a zero profile in ground aerodynamic infrastructure installed flush with highway medians, corniches and critical-facility perimeters. Three coupled sub systems are described: (A) a NACA type flush intake and convergent duct that ingests the surface boundary layer and accelerates it according to A₁v₁ = A₂v₂; (B) a passive multi-cyclone separator that removes quartz sand by centrifugal sedimentation with a Stokes-based cut off diameter d₅₀; and (C) a sealed sub-grade cross flow turbine driving a permanent-magnet generator that feeds an emergency microgrid. We formulate the continuity Bernoulli relations, a pressure budget closure that bounds the attainable throat velocity, the ducted power equation P = ½ρA₂v₂³·CP·ηₘ·ηₑ, and the cyclone cut off model. A worked design point (35 m/s reference wind at 10 m height) closes the pressure budget with a small margin, yields d₅₀ ≈ 12.5 µm and a mass efficiency above 92 % for particles larger than 50 µm, and delivers roughly 1 kW per module, scaling cubically with wind speed. We argue that the value of the SVKH lies in the survivability of critical nodes rather than in energy yield, and we examine civil specifications, siting, avoided loss economics and alignment with UAE Net Zero 2050. This work forms Part II of the Extreme Climatic Kinetic Resilience Series, complementing Part I (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24166640). items.title: Success-Contingent Withdrawal of Diagnostic Scrutiny: How Meeting the Outcome Can End the Question
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Success-Contingent Withdrawal of Diagnostic Scrutiny, a mechanism through which meeting an outcome criterion brings inquiry into a consequential condition to a close. The condition may be a warning that accompanied the result, or something that helped produce a success people hope to repeat. In either case, the immediate result gives people a reason to stop examining a question whose answer still matters for later performance. The paper identifies the evidence needed to trace that withdrawal. What counted as success? What had people learned about the condition itself? Would they have continued to investigate it if the outcome had fallen short? The sequence of events leaves the reason for closure open. Evidence must connect the successful result to the decision to end scrutiny. When the task concerns only the immediate outcome and no consequential question remains open, meeting the criterion can reasonably end the inquiry. The paper places the mechanism alongside Diane Vaughan’s account of the normalization of deviance and examines two documented cases. Ducati entered its first MotoGP season in 2003 intending to learn how to build a better bike. Francesca Gino and Gary Pisano report that unexpected racing success shifted the team’s attention toward winning. It analyzed little of the data it had collected to understand what produced its results. At Barings, an internal audit warned that Nick Leeson controlled both trading and settlement in Singapore. The bank left the recommended separation of duties unimplemented. The subsequent banking inquiry found that Leeson’s reported profitability made managers reluctant to intervene. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper asks who can keep a warning open and who bears the risk when scrutiny ends. A potential application in human–AI evaluation arises when a reviewer flags a citation because the passage may not support an AI-generated answer. If the reviewer closes the flag because the answer matches the benchmark key, the score explains why scrutiny ended. Checking the passage would resolve the outstanding question about support.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is defined in various ways. A machine that enables a more effective way to replace humans in the labor market is one way to define AI. Evaluating external inputs and using it to tackle specific tasks is another way to see AI. With the diversity of definitions, artificial intelligence is generally understood as a tool that helps solve problems, be it personal or professional. Several years ago, before the release of AI applications, people observed how AI worked via personal assistants: Cortana, Siri etc. This is how AI was used at its early stages. Companies started to adopt AI to excel manufacturing and operational tasks, minimizing expenses for labor and excluding human factor at production. Some implement AI for demand and forecast purposes. Sectors of government use AI for their own needs. Healthcare sector with the help of AI improve accuracy of determining patients' diagnoses, massive data facilitates more appropriate personal treatment. In the education sector AI is limited, because it exposes students to losing critical thinking and autonomy. However, students are being taught how to use AI, their knowledge about the technology is being greatly expanded. Focusing on fundamental principles of AI facilitates student's involvement in AI-use. In manufacturing the technology has established its efficacy, through forecast tools, machine-deviation analysis in workflow. Given its moderate cost AI became primary tool not only within big companies, but also amongst small and medium-sized manufacturers.

items.title: SWITCHING: Objective switching inside agents — eight transition propositions instantiated at agent scale, and what the human parallel does and does not show
items.abstract: The transition theory of the LESS–IS–MORE series asks how an economy's effective objective switches: IS derives eight propositions (S1–S8) about measurement gates, ratchets, windows, counter-coalitions, and verification decay from human-economy cases. Here we instantiate the same switching problem inside AI agents, where the operative objective is directly measurable under a rationality gate and the "incumbent coalition" is literal — a weight-committed default no text can out-organise. Using 4,164 audit records across 30 open-weight systems plus four trained intervention checkpoints, we measure switching under five levers: request-level mandates, revised charters, priced settlement, hard runtime gates, and weight-level grafting. The propositions transfer with one systematic refinement: agents decompose into carrier layers — avowed, dispositional, and operative — that can hold different objective values simultaneously, so a transition must name its target layer. Mandates switch the operative of mandate-readers (ΔfB=+0.68) but not committed poles (Δ=0); gates switch behavior on the enforced surface without changing either belief layer; only grafts move the dispositional carrier (fB: 0.75 lexicographic vs 0.30–0.40 maximin) while leaving avowal untouched. Generational chains show a subtler verification-decay signature than S7 predicts: the instrument layer stays verbally intact while the effective layer reverts — verification attached to the declared layer masks the reversal it was meant to catch. The human parallel is real but disciplined: greenwashing's disclosure–performance gap, protected-area designation without enforcement, and ESG-rating divergence exhibit the same three signatures, making agents the first system in which both sides of that gap are measurable and the intervention ethically graftable — a model organism for transition science, not an identity claim. Part of the LESS–IS–MORE program.

items.title: Systematic review of artificial intelligence for personalized oral anticoagulation management in cardiovascular care
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning are increasingly used to personalize oral anticoagulation. We systematically reviewed patient-level studies in adults actively receiving warfarin, vitamin K antagonists, or direct oral anticoagulants. PubMed, Europe PMC, and Scopus were searched from inception to 15 August 2026. Of 984 records, 54 studies met eligibility criteria after duplicate removal, title and abstract screening, and full-text assessment. Applications included dose optimization and anticoagulation control, prediction of bleeding and thromboembolic outcomes, and individualized treatment selection. Warfarin dominated dose-optimization research, whereas direct oral anticoagulants were more prominent in risk and comparative-treatment modelling. Across the evidence base, limited external validation, inconsistent calibration, and sparse prospective evaluation restricted clinical translation. AI-enabled anticoagulation is progressing from static prediction toward longitudinal and treatment-specific decision support, but robust multicentre validation remains essential.

items.title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
items.abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.

items.title: Tawjih: Directing a Language Model with Three-Sided Files and Cross-Tree Production Paths
items.abstract: Working paper describing version 0.6.1 of Tawjih, a file-based method for directing a language model from organized personal knowledge, with a reference implementation in a single Python file that uses only the standard library. Knowledge is kept in trees of small files. Each file has three sides: the human concept, machine language (instructions for the model and Python code), and a reading side holding passages filtered from deposited books. At build time the reading side is turned into the concept and the concept into machine language; at run time only machine language is sent. A path connects files from any tree with the words TO, AND, IF, AMONG and THROUGH. Version 0.6.1 adds data contracts between steps, detection of machine language that is older than its sources, a cache of model answers so a failed run can resume, drawing and generation of paths, a time limit for code steps, and the reading of books from their source formats (Markdown, LaTeX, HTML and PreTeXt XML) so that mathematics survives. The paper reports a trial on two chapters of an open algebra textbook (Judson, Abstract Algebra: Theory and Applications). The author's assistant played the language model through a manual back end, so the trial tests the program and the workflow, not the quality of a model. It exposed six defects, all fixed in this version, and showed that text extracted from the PDF damaged the mathematics while the book's PreTeXt source preserved it. The implementation passes 97 automated tests on Linux and Windows. No evaluation with a small local model has been made yet. Source code: https://github.com/AlmodinyMk/LLM-tawjih-Model-building

items.title: Teachers’ and Students’ Perspectives on the Use of ChatGPT in the Research Methods Course: A Study at Abu-Issa College of Education, University of Zawia, Libya
items.abstract: This study investigated teachers’ and students’ perspectives on the use of ChatGPT in the Research Methods course at Abu-Issa College of Education, University of Zawia. It aimed to explore students’ perceptions of ChatGPT, examine teachers’ views, identify its perceived benefits and challenges, and consider ways of promoting its responsible use in research-related learning. The study adopted a mixed-methods research design. Quantitative data were collected through an online questionnaire administered to 30 seventh-semester students from the English Language Department, while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews with five teachers who had taught the Research Methods course. The questionnaire data were analysed using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, and mean scores, whereas the interview responses were examined thematically. The findings revealed that students generally held positive perceptions of ChatGPT and considered it a useful supplementary learning tool. Almost all students (96.7%) reported having used ChatGPT, while 90% indicated that they had used it for course-related purposes. Students particularly valued its ability to generate research ideas, develop research questions, explain difficult concepts, organise information, and improve academic writing. However, the findings also highlighted concerns regarding inaccurate information, unreliable references, excessive dependence on AI-generated responses, and potential negative effects on critical thinking and independent learning. Teachers similarly acknowledged its educational potential but emphasised the risks of copying generated content without sufficient understanding or critical evaluation. Furthermore, 73.3% of students reported receiving no formal guidance or training on responsible ChatGPT use. The study concludes that ChatGPT can support teaching and learning in Research Methods when accompanied by appropriate guidance, critical evaluation, academic integrity, and independent thinking. It recommends providing students with practical training and establishing clear institutional guidelines for its responsible integration into higher education.

items.title: Teachers’ Professional Fulfillment in STEM Education: Sources, Enablers, and Constraints among Chinese Primary and Secondary STEM Teachers
items.abstract: Teachers’ professional fulfillment in STEM education remains underexplored, particularly regarding the experiences teachers find rewarding and the conditions that support or constrain them. Guided by the meaningful work framework, this study examined responses to two open-ended questions from a survey of 3,959 Chinese primary and secondary teachers. Following data screening, 2,953 teachers were included in a deductive–inductive qualitative content analysis supported by large language model–assisted coding and independent human reliability checks. Five sources of professional fulfillment were identified: student growth and learning, teachers’ professional growth, recognition and relational affirmation, meaning and social value, and intrinsic rewards of STEM teaching. Student-related experiences were perceived as both sources of fulfillment and enabling or constraining factors. Insufficient instructional resources, limited professional learning opportunities, workload, and examination-oriented evaluation emerged as prominent constraints, whereas institutional support and recognition were more frequently described as enabling. A small subset of teachers also described how these conditions restricted, sustained, or expanded their STEM teaching practices. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing professionally rewarding experiences from the conditions that enable or constrain opportunities to realize them.

items.title: Technology-Mediated Language Translation for Older Adults: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Many older adults come from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) communities, where they frequently interact with people and services in multiple languages. Language translation technology can support their multilingual communication. This scoping review examines research on technology-mediated verbal language translation for older adults and provides recommendations for future research and practice. We identified 41 studies across six databases discussing the considerations, development, implementation, and evaluation of various technologies, including mobile apps, artificial intelligence, social robots, internet of things, and handheld translators. Research shows that current technologies offer better accessibility and availability than human interpreters and enable useful functions, including multimodal instant translation, flexible formats, and personalized features. Nevertheless, limitations remain, including mistranslations, disrupted communication, usability concerns, and technical issues. Our findings provide important evidence on the current landscape, opportunities, and considerations for future design (e.g., accuracy, usability, flexibility) and implementation (e.g., environmental control, technical appropriateness, adequate learning) of this technology.

items.title: Tell Me How Sure You Are: Communicating Uncertainty in Auxiliary Evidence to Foundation Models
items.abstract: In many queries, the context information provided to generative foundation models, such as LLMs and VLMs, is inherently uncertain, including its representations of the physical world. While conventional prompting discards the associated uncertainty, this paper, for the first time in the literature, systematically demonstrates that communicating such uncertainty in context provides useful additional cues for downstream decisions and yields improvements across a wide range of settings. We formulate the decision-making problem as a zero-shot foundation model-assisted image classification task supported by auxiliary text-based characteristics. We choose this due to the availability of well-defined auxiliary properties, associated uncertainty, and unambiguous task correctness. Using five downstream foundation models across three datasets, we extensively evaluate uncertainty arising from both humans and learned models when observing or predicting auxiliary evidence. Across all settings, we find that communicating uncertainty substantially improves downstream LLM classification performance: macro-F1 improves up to $26.18$ percentage points compared to when the uncertainty information is not communicated. We further observe how the foundation models process such uncertainty information and find that auxiliary uncertainty contains predictive information about the correctness of downstream decisions. Together, these results establish uncertainty as useful contextual information and motivate more systematic consideration of uncertainty communication in future foundation-model inference pipelines.

items.title: The acmeological gamification framework for creative competence development: a testable theory for pre-service teacher education
items.abstract: Gamification in higher education has been studied mainly as a means of increasing motivation, engagement, and achievement, with far less attention to how game mechanics contribute to the creative competence of pre-service teachers. This article advances the Acmeological Gamification Framework for Creative Competence Development (AGF-CCD), a testable developmental theory of how gamified learning conditions may contribute to creative professional capability in teacher education. The framework was developed through a purposive narrative theory-building synthesis, supported by a mechanism-level evidence map in which empirical studies, syntheses, and theoretical sources are kept apart; it is neither a systematic review nor an empirical validation. It takes the well-supported link from need-supportive mechanics to autonomous motivation as a boundary premise and proposes three sequential links: autonomous motivation is channelled by interpretive feedback into reflective practice and in-task metacognitive regulation (P1); reflective practice under psychological safety and meaningful challenge activates divergent and convergent thinking (P2); and repeated, reflected creative activity in authentic professional tasks consolidates into durable creative competence, evidenced by retention and transfer (P3). Three boundary conditions concern the learner (P4a), the design, separating mechanic composition from framing (P4b), and the context, including teaching discipline (P4c). Relative to self-determination theory, the theory of gamified learning, and the interconnected model of professional growth, the framework's distinctive contribution lies in additional mechanisms (feedback architecture and consolidation), predictions that differ from those accounts (cumulative trajectory; reversal under controlling design), and explicit failure conditions. Acmeology is retained only as a falsifiable claim that development is cumulative. A validation roadmap, including a non-gamified reflective control, states how each proposition can be confirmed, qualified, or refuted.

items.title: The association between different types of anthropomorphism of artificial intelligence service agents and user trust: A three-level meta-analysis
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence service agents (AISAs) become increasingly widespread, anthropomorphism is often proposed as a way to foster user trust, yet empirical findings remain mixed. Drawing on competing trust-building and trust-undermining mechanisms, we conducted a three-level meta-analysis of 211 effect sizes from 136 independent samples ( N = 46,071) to estimate the anthropomorphism–trust association and examine its boundary conditions. The average association was positive and robust to alternative dependence models ( r = 0.462, 95% CI [0.420, 0.502]), but varied substantially across settings (95% prediction interval [−0.131, 0.811]). It was considerably weaker for objectively specified design cues ( r = 0.222) than for perception-based measures ( r = 0.543), most of which captured adjacent trait attributions such as competence and warmth. Restricting outcomes to global trust, reliance, or willingness to depend yielded a similar estimate ( r = 0.475), although construct overlap on the outcome side cannot be ruled out. Cognitive and emotional anthropomorphism were more strongly associated with trust than physical anthropomorphism in aggregate, but this difference was no longer significant after adjusting for operationalization; among design cues, physical and emotional anthropomorphism did not differ significantly, and no design-based cognitive effect sizes were available. The association was stronger in Eastern than in Western samples and in survey than in experimental studies, whereas no statistically significant moderation was detected for gender composition or the prespecified service-context categories. These findings caution against reading the pooled association as a uniform effect of anthropomorphic design and suggest that anthropomorphic cues should complement, rather than substitute for, demonstrable competence and reliability in AISA design and deployment.

items.title: The cloud is not weightless: data-centre infrastructure, urban surface conditions, and governance across 200 global urban centres
items.abstract: Introduction Growth in cloud services and artificial-intelligence computing has intensified policy attention to the physical infrastructure of data centres. The empirical exposure is not AI-specific: PeeringDB does not consistently identify workload, GPU or HPC deployment, IT load, electricity capacity, cooling demand, or the share of a facility devoted to AI-related computation. The study therefore examines ecological associations with current PeeringDB-listed facility records while retaining a broader set of panel, spatial, distributional, and facility-centred analyses to assess uncertainty and heterogeneity. Methods The study uses 200 fixed-2025 GHSL Urban Centre polygons and 1,400 annual observations from 2019 to 2025. Facility count means the number of current PeeringDB-listed facility records with valid coordinates inside the relevant polygon. The primary models relate log(1 + facility count) to 2025 NDVI, McFeeters NDWI, and NDBI, condition 2025 outcomes on their corresponding 2019 values, and examine 2023–2025 means. Two-part models separate matched-record presence from the listing-count gradient among 131 positive-listing centres. Secondary analyses retain the repeated panel, Urban Centre fixed-effects trajectories, alternative exposure and sample definitions, bootstrap and multiple-testing checks, regional, quantile, hierarchical, and spatial models, and 2 km and 5 km profiles around 26 audited facilities. Seven facilities have directly verified timing for descriptive event profiles. Results The primary full-sample models do not show significant associations between current facility count and 2025 NDVI, McFeeters NDWI, or NDBI, and the conclusion is unchanged after the 2019 starting-condition adjustment and in 2023–2025 means. Matched-record presence is also null. Among positive-listing centres, the simple 2025 count gradient is positive for NDVI and negative for NDWI, but the NDWI coefficient attenuates from −0.021 ( p = 0.006) to −0.002 ( p = 0.243) after 2019 NDWI is included. In the repeated 2019–2025 panel, the global NDWI coefficient remains borderline and the fixed-effects trajectory models do not show a stable adverse pattern. Distributional, regional, and spatial models reproduce a negative conditional NDWI association in some specifications, while the seven directly timed facilities show no common post-opening satellite signature. Discussion The primary design does not detect a robust adverse ecological association between current PeeringDB facility count and near-contemporaneous city-wide surface conditions. The broader analytical package is retained because it shows where patterns recur, where they disappear, and which conclusions depend on modelling choices. The conditional NDWI association remains mechanistically unresolved and is substantially connected to earlier NDWI conditions. None of the analyses identifies facility openings, AI-specific effects, cooling-water withdrawal, groundwater depletion, or municipal water stress. City-wide non-detection also cannot establish safety or exclude parcel- and neighbourhood-scale effects.

items.title: The Comprehension Gap in LLM-Assisted Software Development: An Experiment
items.abstract: When LLM tools are pushed beyond their capabilities for software development tasks, developers must be able to step in. However, the comprehension that developers acquire during development might be negatively impacted due to excessive code generation. This could create a cognitive debt that needs to be resolved before tasks can be solved efficiently again. We explore how well developers understand code they generated by prompting in comparison to self-written and unseen code and how they reflect on their comprehension. We conduct a crossover experiment and interviews with 35 participants consisting of students, academic personnel, and software developers. After completing two programming tasks with or without LLM chat usage, respectively, participants are tasked with finding introduced mutations in the produced and additional unseen code. We use insights from interviews and screen recordings to supplement our results. Regarding the experiment, 36% of participants report a better understanding of self-written code compared to their generated code. On average, participants solved the comprehension task 20% faster for self-written code than for generated code and found 11% more mutations. Participants needed significantly less time to solve programming tasks when working with the LLM. However, participants with high reliance on the LLM chat and low task engagement showed significantly decreased comprehension. Our qualitative results show great variability in individual perspectives on comprehension differences and strategies to mitigate issues. Strategies for dealing with comprehension differences range from accepting comprehension differences to adapting their LLM interactions or avoiding the tools altogether. Our results warrant further investigation into cognitive debt in larger systems and developer practices to mitigate issues.

items.title: The Digital Eye in Plant Disease Surveillance: A Critical Synthesis of Imaging, Artificial Intelligence and Smart Diagnosis
items.abstract: Plant disease surveillance is moving from episodic visual inspection towards image-supported observation across leaves, crop canopies and landscapes. Digital cameras, spectral and thermal sensors, uncrewed aerial vehicles and artificial intelligence have expanded the measurable manifestations of plant stress, yet the ability to recognise a pattern is not equivalent to identifying its cause or improving disease management. This critical narrative review examines the evidence linking imaging modalities, computational models and diagnostic workflows to operational surveillance. Peer-reviewed studies and methodological reviews published from 2010 to 10 September 2026 were considered, with earlier concepts addressed where necessary. The synthesis evaluates sensor-specific biological signals, experimental design, dataset provenance, cross-domain generalisation, object detection and severity estimation, aerial and satellite monitoring, and the role of human and laboratory verification. Controlled-image classification has demonstrated substantial technical feasibility, but independent field evaluations frequently reveal reductions in recall and weak transportability across sites, cultivars, seasons and acquisition devices. Spectral and thermal measurements can detect altered physiology before obvious visual injury in selected experiments; nevertheless, such responses are seldom pathogen-specific and may be confounded by abiotic stress or crop development. Multi-scale mapping can locate suspected disease foci, although spatial resolution, timing, sampling design and ground-truth uncertainty constrain interpretation. Recent advances in domain adaptation, multimodal learning, anomaly detection and explainability are promising but have not consistently established prospective diagnostic or management value. The review proposes a surveillance-oriented framework that separates detection, aetiological diagnosis, severity estimation, forecasting and intervention. Progress depends less on marginal improvements in benchmark accuracy than on independent prospective evaluation, calibrated uncertainty, representative datasets, expert-mediated confirmation and measurements of decisions and outcomes. Digital imaging is best understood as an additional evidential layer within plant health surveillance rather than a stand-alone substitute for plant pathology.

items.title: THE ECONOMIC VALUE OF LIFELONG LEARNING IN THE DIGITAL ECONOMY: LEVERAGING SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH AND TECHNOLOGICAL TOOLS FOR HUMAN CAPITAL DEVELOPMENT
items.abstract: Abstract Digital transformation is fundamentally changing not only the technological foundations of the economy but also the demands placed on the workforce. The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence, big data, cloud technologies, automation and digital platforms requires employees to acquire new knowledge and skills continuously, update their existing competencies and adapt to a changing labour market. From this perspective, lifelong learning is emerging as a long-term mechanism for developing human capital. This article examines, from theoretical and analytical perspectives, the economic significance of lifelong learning in the digital economy and the impact of scientific research and modern technological tools on human capital performance. The study uses systems analysis, comparative analysis, logical generalisation, an institutional approach, and the interpretation of available international statistical and analytical materials. Drawing on contemporary sources related to the OECD, the European Commission and European education policy, lifelong learning is considered a process associated with economic growth, labour productivity, innovation, digital transformation and improvements in the quality of employment. The findings indicate that lifelong learning should be viewed not merely as a task of the education sector, but as an interconnected component of economic policy, labour-market policy, innovation-driven development and digital transformation. The article substantiates the conceptual chain "scientific research → technological tools → lifelong learning → human capital → labour productivity → innovation → economic growth". It also analyses digital learning platforms, artificial intelligence, micro-credentials, online learning and personalised learning tools as important instruments for improving the effectiveness of lifelong learning.

items.title: The Economics of AI and Robotics: A Scenario Analysis of Automation, Employment, Poverty, Taxation and Income Distribution in a Hypothetical Three-Sector Economy
items.abstract: This study examines how the deepening of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics, defined as the progressive replacement of human workers by machines, affects output, employment, poverty and income distribution. Drawing on the economics of prediction and general-purpose technologies, the task-based theory of automation, growth theory, the literature on factor shares and Keynesian demand constraints, we construct a hypothetical economy, Solvania, with 30 million inhabitants, GDP per capita of US$25,000, 6% unemployment, a 5.3% poverty rate and three sectors: agriculture (30% of output and employment), automobile manufacturing (20%) and services (50%). A macro-sectoral model linked to a 150,000-household microsimulation, implemented in Python, traces a gradual scenario, in which automation reaches 25% of jobs within five years and 50% by year 20, and a rapid scenario, in which it reaches 80% in agriculture and manufacturing and 60% in services within ten years. Both paths raise GDP strongly, to US$1.57 trillion by year 20 (gradual) and US$1.39 trillion by year 10 (rapid), but the gains are distributed very unequally. In the rapid scenario unemployment reaches 47.2%, the labour share falls from 60% to 19.9%, the Gini coefficient rises from 0.369 to 0.621 and poverty more than triples to 17.3%, while median income rises by only 8%. A policy package combining an automation levy that finances a universal dividend, universal income support, accelerated reinstatement and work sharing reduces poverty to 0.7%, lowers the Gini to 0.408 and raises GDP by a further 16%. The results are robust to alternative assumptions and support redistributive and labour market institutions established before the fastest phase of automation. items.title: The Emerging Role and Integration of Artificial Intelligence Tools in Veterinary Education: A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), a data-driven and algorithm-supported technological system, has rapidly expanded its role in transforming daily life and professional practice over the past decade. In this narrative review, the recent literature was examined to evaluate current and emerging applications of AI in veterinary education and practice. A previously reported PubMed-focused search and a broader literature compilation served different purposes. The historical screening counts cannot be fully reconstructed, and the synthesis was narrative rather than systematic. Veterinary schools in the United States and elsewhere have begun exploring and integrating AI into Doctor of Veterinary Medicine (DVM) curricula to support teaching, learning, and competency development. This review summarizes recent advances in the application of AI in veterinary education. In anatomy, AI-based visualization and interactive tools are being explored, although controlled evidence of improved learning outcomes remains limited. In digital pathology, AI-assisted image analysis can provide students with opportunities to develop skills in recognizing and interpreting pathological findings. In clinical settings, AI models have shown potential in selected imaging and clinical-classification tasks, but their educational effectiveness requires further evaluation. Despite these advances, the broader implementation of AI in veterinary education and practice faces important regulatory and ethical challenges, including concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, academic integrity, and the reliability of AI-generated information. Addressing these issues will require multidisciplinary collaboration, multicenter data integration, appropriate validation, and strong ethical governance. With these foundations in place, AI may serve as a supportive educational and clinical tool rather than a replacement for veterinary educators and professionals. In the future, appropriately validated AI tools may contribute to veterinary education and clinical training.

items.title: The Empty Chair in AI Governance: Why Human Oversight may Fail When we Need it Most
items.abstract: AI governance frameworks increasingly rely on the assurance that a “human in the loop” will provide accountability, judgment, and control when artificial intelligence systems are used in consequential decisions. This paper argues that this assurance is incomplete and potentially misleading unless organizations examine whether the human system surrounding the AI is actually capable of exercising judgment when it matters. The paper defines artificial intelligence as machine inference: computational systems that detect patterns, generate outputs, recommend actions, and simulate features of reasoning without conscience, responsibility, embodiment, or wisdom. It introduces the concept of the Empty Chair: the absence of a clearly designated owner for the formation, sustainment, and exercise of human judgment in AI-enabled decision systems. The paper proposes that meaningful oversight requires at least seven conditions: cognitive capability, behavioral authority, relational safety, decision discipline, cognitive sustainment, survivability, and relational sustainment. Drawing on applied organizational work with governance bodies, enterprise leaders, public-facing institutional systems, and cross-organizational cohorts, the paper identifies a recurring capability-authority split in which those most likely to detect certain categories of risk are not always positioned or authorized to interrupt decision momentum. The analysis further examines how automation bias and ethical fading can weaken human responsibility by making AI outputs appear more complete, objective, and procedurally sufficient than they are. The paper reframes cognitive diversity as governance infrastructure rather than a team-building concept and presents the D.E.E.P.E.R.™ practice as a structured method for recurring reflective diversification across decision cycles. It also offers practical interventions, including cognitive diversity audits, cognitive role charters, decision pause points, Empty Chair protocols, authority alignment, and recurring reflective practice. The paper concludes that AI governance cannot stop at governing machines. It must also govern the human systems responsible for supervising them. The central question is not whether a human is present in the loop, but whether that human is formed, positioned, protected, sustained, and authorized to exercise judgment under pressure.

items.title: The Future of AI & XR: How Will AI Reshape the Spatial Computing Pipeline?
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping how extended reality environments are created, experienced, and applied. Advances in generative AI, multimodal foundation models, spatial understanding, embodied intelligence, and wearable technologies create new opportunities across the spatial computing pipeline, but also raise questions concerning human agency, accessibility, trust, and responsible design. This workshop brings together researchers and practitioners from artificial intelligence, computer graphics, human-computer interaction, and extended reality to examine these developments through three complementary perspectives: AI-generated worlds for XR, human-centred interaction, and human augmentation. Invited experts will introduce these perspectives through brief position statements, followed by moderated panel discussions involving speakers and attendees. Interactive breakout sessions will enable participants to identify connections across the three perspectives, discuss open challenges, and formulate promising directions for future research. By combining expert viewpoints with active community participation, the workshop aims to foster interdisciplinary exchange and initiate a broader community effort towards a shared research agenda for the future of AI and XR.

items.title: The General Practitioner as Institutional Polymath: A Hypothesis on What Artificial Intelligence Changes in Breadth, Depth and Integration
items.abstract: General practice asks ordinary practitioners to combine breadth across all health problems, depth in the field and in the continuing care of persons, and integration within the single consultation. Drawing on a recent triadic model of polymathy, in which breadth, depth and integration are jointly necessary and the term can refer to any system that displays them, this hypothesis paper proposes to describe the general practitioner as an institutional polymath: a role, rather than a person, whose defining documents require all three dimensions and whose training is designed to produce them in ordinary practitioners. In the author's reading of the twelve characteristics of the European Definition of General Practice/Family Medicine, breadth and integration are primary in several characteristics, depth is required both in the field and in the person, and no characteristic refers to digital or artificial intelligence (AI) tools. Drawing on evidence from general practice and from research on reliance on automated advice, the paper hypothesises that AI currently lowers the cost of stored breadth but not of integration or of checking, that the ability to detect wrong outputs depends on the practitioner's depth of medical knowledge, and that this depth may weaken with use of the tool. Studies in which AI systems matched or exceeded physicians, and a meta-analysis in which human-AI combinations performed, on average, worse than the better of the two, are discussed as counter-evidence. The central hypothesis is that competence for AI use in general practice is better described as maintaining the triad under new conditions than as a set of digital skills alone. The paper derives a specific prediction from the conjunctive model, an interaction between practitioner knowledge, AI support and the correctness of the suggestion, specifies five observations that would refute or narrow the hypothesis, and states eleven hypothesised competencies, each paired with an observation that would count against it. It makes no clinical recommendations and outlines a Delphi study and empirical tests.

items.title: The Impact of Transformational Leadership and Organizational Culture on Employee Performance: A Study of a Selected Company in Malaysia
items.abstract: Employee performance is a central determinant of organizational productivity, service quality, and competitiveness, particularly in the fast-changing Malaysian business environment. This paper examines how transformational leadership and organizational culture are theorized and empirically associated with employee performance, and it develops a research framework and testable hypotheses for a survey-based investigation in a selected Malaysian company. Drawing on transformational leadership theory (Bass, 1985; Bass & Riggio, 2006), Schein's model of organizational culture (Schein & Schein, 2017), and social exchange theory (Cropanzano & Mitchell, 2005), the study positions transformational leadership and organizational culture as independent variables and employee performance as the dependent variable. A systematic review of Malaysian and international empirical studies indicates consistent positive associations between transformational leadership behaviors, particularly idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration, and employee performance outcomes, as well as between supportive organizational cultures and higher performance. The paper details a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design using validated instruments (the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire, the Organizational Culture Assessment Instrument, and the Individual Work Performance Questionnaire), a Krejcie and Morgan-based sample-size procedure, and a planned analytical strategy combining descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression. Four hypotheses are proposed linking transformational leadership and organizational culture, individually and jointly, to employee performance. The paper concludes with theoretical and managerial implications, arguing that Malaysian organizations seeking to improve workforce productivity should invest jointly in leadership development and culture-building initiatives rather than treating them as separate interventions. Limitations of single-organization, cross-sectional designs and directions for future longitudinal and multi-sector research are discussed.

items.title: The importance of a general practice placement in postgraduate medical training: Finnish junior doctors’ perspectives
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Experience in general practice is considered a valuable component of postgraduate medical training. It is well-established in the Nordic countries. In Finland, a nine-month general practice placement is included in postgraduate medical training. However, there is limited research on assessing its importance for junior doctors. OBJECTIVES: To investigate how junior doctors perceive and experience the importance of the nine-month general practice placement, and their experiences of working as a primary care physician. METHODS: We conducted a qualitative study including focus group interviews and qualitative content analysis. RESULTS: A total of 14 junior doctors participated. We defined ten themes describing junior doctors' perceptions and experiences. The themes were categorised according to the framework by Biesta into three functions of education: qualification, socialisation, and subjectification. According to the qualification function, the placement is relevant for junior doctors. It develops the physician's essential competencies and provides an understanding of the primary care field. The socialisation function highlights the importance of workplace learning and the core principles of general practice. The subjectification function emphasises work management and the development of future career plans. Work in primary care is considered busy and demanding, but also rewarding and diverse, offering comprehensive patient relationships. CONCLUSIONS: This study emphasises the valuable role of the general practice placement in postgraduate medical education in Finland. The findings underscore the importance of comprehensive professional development, workplace learning, and work management among junior doctors. The placement provides an overview of primary healthcare, enables career planning, and promotes appreciation for general practitioners.

items.title: The limits of declarative authorship: the structural vulnerability of intellectual property in the age of generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI functions as a near zero cost execution engine, weakening the long standing reliance on human effort on which traditional intellectual property (IP) systems depend. The academic response has focused, so far, on studying productivity at the micro level, debating the doctrinal question of IP infringement through AI training at the macro level, or blunt denial of AI authorship. These responses miss the central problem: the human provenance at the heart of IP law is now cheap to falsify and hard to verify. In this paper I argue that AI output appropriation poses a significant threat to IP through an adverse selection dynamic. The threat comes from humans who use AI to appropriate its output and extract the value attached to human effort. Skill compression effects cutting across writing, coding, and consulting have begun to commoditize execution, compressing the quality distribution that once supported premium prices for IP protected output. This process is compounded by the difficulty of verifying declared human authorship or inventorship, which may reward deception and discourage honest effort. I therefore explore value migration from execution skill to concentrated complementary assets. Building on market evidence from platform economies, the paper considers an evolution of IP from a rights based asset model to a verification model, in which the human role shifts from creator to authenticator.

items.title: The Machine Notary: Cryptographic Intersubjectivity and the Foundation of the Agent Economy
items.abstract: Current AI agent architectures operate on subjective, mutable memory without a shared external witness. This paper argues that stable agent economies (money, law, history) require intersubjective reality: shared agreement verified by an external witness. We introduce the Machine Notary, a protocol instantiated by Recallspection's ExactMemory architecture (AGMI L4 conformance, 10/10 attacks rejected). The Machine Notary provides three pillars: cryptographic provenance (who wrote it), continuity (the chain), and consensus (the anchor). Now we makes the claim precise: one canonical math definition used everywhere, an explicit threat model, full AGMI attack list, real anchor cost and liveness rules, arbiter selection with quorum and appeal, and salted tombstones with metadata-leakage analysis. We define the primitives, demonstrate the protocol via an agent-to-agent supply chain scenario, and address dispute resolution, anchor economics, human readability, and crypto-shredding. We conclude with governance mechanisms to prevent a subjective dictatorship of centralized anchors.This paper is the policy and economic framework for the technical architecture defined in "Synthetic Intelligence Requires Exact Memory" (Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23378369). The Machine Notary is operationalized via the open-source RPRS-1 (Read-Path Refusal Specification) protocol. The technical foundation achieves AGMI Level L4 conformance, rejecting 10/10 storage-level attacks on the read path. The protocol specification & referenceimplementation are available at: https://github.com/sciencedelicmetatech/recallspection

items.title: The Majority Report: AI Optimism and Public Support for Police Use of AI in Nine Countries
items.abstract: Police forces increasingly use Artificial Intelligence in support of specific tasks, such as data analysis, identifying suspects and monitoring public spaces. These uses potentially expand the state’s coercive capacity. Yet we know little about how far people accept these tools across political contexts and how these views systematically relate to other attitudes. We ask whether support rests on views of the technology, the problem AI use addresses, or trust in the institution using it. We analyze a preregistered survey of 9,000 respondents in the United States, China, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and five EU countries using Bayesian multilevel models. Support is high for most uses everywhere. It rests on general AI benefits, perceived crime trends, and trust in the police, which matters similarly across countries. In contrast, general AI risks, personal fear of crime, and trust in legal institutions play no substantive role on average. Acceptance thus primarily is connected with optimism about AI, a general but not personal sense of problem relevance, and trust in the police.

items.title: The Proficiency of Various AI Models Within Deepfake Detection
items.abstract: As AI evolves, it is increasingly challenging to distinguish authentic media from deepfakes. This encourages fraud, misinformation, and legal ambiguity. Despite the existence of specialized deepfake detection tools, consumer-targeted AI agents used by millions have not been systematically evaluated for this task under controlled conditions. This study evaluates the reliability of widespread AI agents in deepfake detection, utilizing human performance as a control group. If AI can generate deepfakes, then it should be equally equipped to detect deepfakes, with a minimum accuracy of 90% across all aspects. To evaluate this, four models were assessed—ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Super Grok—on approximately 300 royalty-free images within four categories: boys, girls, cats, and dogs. To ensure consistency, metadata was stripped using PrivMeta, watermarks were removed with EZRemove V2, file names were randomized with a Java program, and temporary chat sessions were utilized to prevent pattern formation. The decision and confidence score—from 1 to 10—of each AI model were recorded. Three human participants of ages 11, 19, and 48 emulated this for comparison. The hypothesis was disproved by the results. Across all models and trials, the aggregate accuracy on real images was greater than deepfakes, at 89.64% and 65.98% respectively. Gemini demonstrated the greatest performance with an accuracy of 85.79% and also detected deepfakes with more accuracy than real images, at 93.94% and 79.75% respectively. Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok followed with scores of 83.47%, 78.19%, and 68.52% in that order. All models performed better at detecting humans as opposed to animal images. Gender bias was shown towards male faces, with greater accuracy than that of females. These findings reveal that the most publicly-available AI tools are the least qualified to defend against the deepfakes that other AI models generate. As deepfake quality increases, this imbalance reduces public trust of journalism, legal evidence, and political discourse. Reliable deepfake detection should be treated as a premium feature, rather than a public safeguard integrated into the platforms millions use every day.

items.title: The SAFER AI Protocol for operational AI reliance and responsible human verification
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to draft, summarize, classify, forecast, and communicate information in educational and organizational settings. The resulting governance problem is not limited to model error: AI-generated output becomes consequential when a human accepts, reuses, transmits, or acts on it without review proportionate to the context. This conceptual framework article defines operational AI reliance as the workflow-level process by which a person or institution decides whether and how to use AI-generated output as a basis for action. It develops the SAFER AI™ Protocol as a bounded human-reliance governance framework comprising Scope, Authority, Failure Awareness, Evidence, and Record. The framework does not replace technical assurance, legal compliance, model evaluation, privacy or security controls, or system-level accountability. Its contribution is a user-facing decision routine that connects those controls to the post-generation, pre-action point at which output is evaluated. The article reports an interdisciplinary narrative synthesis of Responsible AI governance, human-centered AI, automation bias, trust calibration, AI literacy, socio-technical governance, and organizational accountability. It then operationalizes the framework through defined terms, a traceability model, a contextual risk classification rubric, an evidence depth scale, and a complete decision flow. The paper concludes with bounded applications in higher education and enterprise work, the framework’s failure mechanisms, and an empirical research agenda that distinguishes verification benefits from implementation burdens. The proposed framework remains conceptual and requires independent empirical evaluation.

items.title: The scientist’s AI-pprentice: how open science shapes biosecurity risks by generating capabilities of AI tools in life science research
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly incorporated in the life sciences. Until recently, the need for data governance was masked by the limits of our human ability to aggregate, synthesise, and draw inferences from data. AI enhances not only speed of research and data processing, but also dual-use risks from training AI models with open access data. Concerns about AI-enabled chemical and biological weapons development become louder while governments, institutions and model developers scramble to mitigate and contain those risks. Data remains a crucial ingredient for AI model advancement, consequentially the lack of data governance of AI in life sciences leaves us collectively and personally vulnerable. Traditional data governance controls storage, transfer and access to datasets, but AI-enabled life science research raises a different issue: which novel capabilities emerge when models aggregate and orchestrate openly available data and tools, arising from individually benign contributions and not covered by current governance. Thus, we highlight questions and ethical considerations on which precautions are required when risks arise through data aggregation and re-use, how responsibility can be distributed, whether governance should focus on data or novel capabilities and if openness should cease to be default. Data governance works upstream, before data is introduced to an AI model. It follows that more life science dual-use data of concern should be held in Trusted Research Environments rather than released openly, and that dual-use data assessments become routine, implemented through research funders as chokepoints, to bridge the legislative gap until international dual-use standards are established.

items.title: The Structural and Thematic Landscape of Software Supply Chain Security: A Narrative Review Guided by Synthetic Knowledge Synthesis
items.abstract: The software industry is confronting a critical crisis driven by systemic vulnerabilities within the software supply chain and the ubiquitous reliance on third-party dependencies. While individual exploits and localized compliance frameworks have been heavily studied, this highly fragmented academic discourse creates a critical barrier to organizational readiness and proactive incident preparedness. To address this gap and enhance digital resilience, this study maps the conceptual, knowledge and structural landscape of the software supply chain literature using Synthetic Knowledge Synthesis. The findings provide actionable threat intelligence designed to primarily benefit enterprise security teams, DevSecOps practitioners, and cybersecurity policymakers. Analyzing publications from 2021 to 2026, the research reveals an exponential growth in output, heavily dominated by conference proceedings and driven primarily by institutional and state-funded efforts in the United States and China. Thematic mapping identifies five core clusters defining the current ecosystem: software composition analysis, Advanced Vulnerability Detection, AI-Driven Threat Intelligence, deep learning, and DevSecOps. The study highlights critical unresolved gaps, notably the prevalence of false positives in static software bill of materials tools due to a lack of execution context, and a pronounced disconnect between theoretical models and practical enterprise application. items.title: The Unappreciated Helper: When an AI Facilitation Agent Improves Group Efficiency Despite Poorer User Perceptions
items.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence make it possible to embed AI facilitation agents in collaborative settings, where they can deliver real-time recommendations based on ongoing group discussions. This experimental study examined how group members perceive a collaborative platform with or without such an agent and evaluated the agent’s effects on group communication and performance. A total of 187 undergraduate psychology students collaborated in 50 groups of three or four members on a digital platform with a synchronous text chat. Groups were randomly assigned to one of two conditions (25 groups per condition): with an AI facilitation agent (n = 96 participants) that encouraged information sharing when exchanges were insufficient, or without the agent (n = 91 participants). Participants rated the platform’s acceptability, perceived support, sense of intrusion, and affective reactions. Participants in the AI condition rated the platform as less acceptable and less supportive, but not more intrusive or unpleasant. Nevertheless, groups assisted by the agent were more efficient, completing the task faster with less communicative effort. Descriptive analyses of group interactions in the three minutes before and after the agent’s interventions showed a shift from providing information toward requesting information, expressing opinions, and agreeing, without change in overall interaction volume. These findings reveal a gap between objective performance and subjective perceptions, highlighting the need to design AI agents that improve group efficiency while fostering members’ sense of support and acceptance.

items.title: The Unsituated Interlocutor: Artificial Intelligence and Evaluative Dialogue in Impact Investing
items.abstract: This article examines how evaluative dialogue changes when an evaluation professional's interlocutor is a large language model (LLM) rather than a human colleague. Drawing on interviews, focus groups, and structured reflections from 13 impact investing evaluation practitioners, the study identifies three properties that human interlocutors bring to evaluative dialogue—personal commitments and experience, shared organizational knowledge, and accountability to colleagues—and traces what happens when each is missing. Each absence proved both productive and limiting: LLMs broadened the options considered, exposed uncodified conventions, and reduced the social cost of candor. Yet they could be steered toward nearly any conclusion, could not read unwritten organizational norms, and, with nothing at stake, offered agreement and pushback that carried little weight. Prompting and document uploads compensated only partially. The findings position LLMs as preparatory interlocutors rather than substitutes for collegial exchange and clarify what evaluative dialogue requires of its participants.

items.title: The use of the Six Thinking Hats activity in nursing education for intestinal stoma care: a mixed-methods study of nursing students’ opinions and evaluations
items.abstract: The Six Thinking Hats activity helps students evaluate problems from six different perspectives. The aim of the study was to examine students’ satisfaction with the Six Thinking Hats activity and, their opinions and evaluations on the process, and to jointly evaluate these findings. This is a convergent parallel design mixed-methods study, in which quantitative and qualitative components were conducted. The quantitative phase used a one-group posttest-only design. The qualitative phase involved in-depth interviews. The population of the study consisted of students enrolled in a surgical nursing course during the spring semester of the 2023–2024 academic year at a public university ( N = 117). In the course, Six Thinking Hats activity was implemented in education on the care of patients with intestinal stomas. The quantitative phase was completed with 97 students. For the qualitative phase, criterion sampling was used and 14 students participated. A semistructured individual interview form was used in the qualitative phase. The obtained statements were evaluated with thematic analysis. Students reported significantly higher satisfaction with the Six Thinking Hats activity than with the traditional course method (Z = − 5.271, p < 0.001). For the qualitative phase; 4 categories, 10 themes, and 34 subthemes were identified. The categories included emotions about the activity, the skills/abilities utilized during the activity, and the benefits and difficulties of the activity. The categories included emotions about the activity, the skills/abilities utilized during the activity, and the benefits and difficulties of the activity. Active learning activity appeared to support overall satisfaction by fostering individual cognitive engagement and group-level multi-perspective thinking. At the same time, qualitative results showed an expansion by highlighting both individual and group challenges experienced during the process. The qualitative results also showed an expansion with quantitative scores by revealing students’ awareness of stoma nurse’s professional role and stoma care needs. Findings suggest that the activity may have enhanced student awareness of patient care needs and nursing roles. items.title: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow
items.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.

items.title: This Looks Like What? Challenges and Future Research Directions for Part-Prototype Models
items.abstract: The growing interest in eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has stimulated research on models with built-in interpretability, among which part-prototype models are particularly prominent. Part-Prototype Models (PPMs) classify inputs by comparing them to learned prototypes and provide human-understandable explanations of the form “this looks like that.” Despite this intrinsic interpretability, PPMs have not yet emerged as a competitive alternative to post-hoc explanation methods. This survey reviews work published between 2019 and 2025 and derives a taxonomy of the challenges faced by current PPMs. The analysis reveals a diverse set of open problems. The main issue concerns the quality and number of learned prototypes. Further challenges include limited generalization across tasks and contexts, as well as methodological shortcomings such as non-standardized evaluation. Five broad research directions are identified: improving predictive performance, developing theoretically grounded architectures, establishing frameworks for human-AI collaboration, aligning models with human concepts, and defining robust metrics and benchmarks for evaluation. The survey aims to stimulate further research and promote intrinsically interpretable models for practical applications. A curated list of the surveyed papers is available at https://github.com/aix-group/ppm-survey .

items.title: Three Proposals to Address the Ethical and Educational Challenge of Unexplainable AI Tools
items.abstract: Historically, engineers have been able to certify, explain, and justify the tools they design because they had direct insight into how these tools work. However, the growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) tools, particularly those based on neural networks and other models that are not easily explainable, presents a significant ethical challenge: who takes responsibility when neither engineers can explain the tools’ outcome, nor end users can interpret decisions to make informed actions? This “responsibility gap,” caused by the lack of explainability in AI within the context of its increasingly widespread use, demands urgent strategies to mitigate the negative effects of its potential unethical implementations. This article presents a three-tiered approach to reduce the impact of algorithmic opacity: (1) raising social awareness and providing education on the limitations of unexplainable AI systems, (2) creating sector-specific ethical frameworks to guide when (if ever) it is appropriate to use these tools, and (3) establishing a standardized labeling system to indicate the potential limitations and biases of these technologies. Each proposal is evaluated using the AREA framework from Responsible Research & Innovation (Anticipate, Reflect, Engage, Act), allowing us to assess its ethical robustness, societal relevance, and implementation feasibility. The result is a set of conceptual tools designed not to eliminate opacity, but to make it visible, interpretable, and ethically manageable across diverse domains of use.

items.title: TimeSeek: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Pretraining for Generalized Time Series Analytics
items.abstract: Time series analytics has been widely applied across various domains. While existing time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated promising results, they still face two major challenges: 1) Most TSFMs mainly rely on stacking Transformer layers to increase parameter size, lacking the ability to adaptively model complex time series patterns from multi-domain data. 2) Current TSFMs are primarily pre-trained for specific tasks, e.g., forecasting or anomaly detection, and a few models support multiple tasks, but they fail to fully leverage task specificity and commonality, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose TimeSeek, a novel generalized time series analytics model that adaptively models time series patterns from multi-domain data and unifies multiple tasks in pre-training. Conceptually, TimeSeek is guided by selective information sharing under domain and task heterogeneity. From the perspective of multi-domain data, we propose a Multi-Domain Feature Extractor that adaptively captures temporal dependencies and channel correlations based on domain-specific characteristics, including progressive multi-scale modeling and adaptive slot channel modeling. From the perspective of the diversity of tasks, we propose multi-task collaborative training, which leverages task specificity and task commonality through task customization and cross-task training, effectively unifying multiple tasks in pre-training and better adapting to diverse downstream scenarios. After pre-training on large-scale time series data, TimeSeek achieves state-of-the-art performance in forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification tasks across both few-shot learning and zero-shot situations, together with favorable inference efficiency.

items.title: TOK TOK: Human Direction, Visual Consistency, and Productive Unpredictability in Generative AI Animation
items.abstract: TOK TOK is a four-minute generative AI animated short about a blind man and his elderly guide dog. After fifteen years of serving as the man’s eyes, the dog’s own sight begins to fade, and the man returns to a long-unused white cane. This practice-based report examines productive unpredictability: a method in which deviations between intention and generated output become creative material only after passing through human judgment. GPT Image 2 was used to develop visual references; Seedance 2.5 generated moving images, sound effects, and ambient audio; and CapCut was used for editing. A fixed reference system constrained character and environmental identity across independently generated shots. Unexpected movements were assessed against the emotional and narrative function of each shot and retained, rejected, or regenerated accordingly. Retained departures could inform subsequent shots and acquire meaning through editing and sound. The case suggests that authorship in generative animation is exercised through decisions about which generated results are retained, rejected, and given meaning in context.

items.title: Toward AI Leadership: A Systematic Literature Review of Leadership Behaviors Enacted by Conversational Agents in Psychosocial Interventions
items.abstract: This project is a systematic literature review that investigates how conversational agents (CAs; e.g., chatbots and virtual assistants) enact leadership-equivalent behaviors in psychosocial interventions, including therapy, counseling, and coaching. Advances in artificial intelligence have enabled these systems to move beyond process automation and engage in adaptive, relational, and motivational dialogue with users. As such, they increasingly perform functions that parallel those of human leaders, raising important theoretical and practical questions about the nature of leadership when enacted by nonhuman agents. The review has three main purposes. First, it examines which leadership behaviors are effectively exhibited by conversational agents, using Yukl et al.’s (2012) taxonomy of task-, relationship-, change-, and externally-oriented behaviors as an organizing framework. Second, it investigates the mechanisms through which these behaviors exert influence on users in psychosocial contexts, and identifies points of divergence from human-enacted leadership theory. Third, it distills methodological lessons from the existing evidence base, particularly regarding causal trustworthiness, intervention transparency, and replicability, to inform the design of future AI leadership research. The evidence base for this review draws primarily from rigorous experimental and longitudinal studies in medical and behavioral sciences, which provide a strong foundation for assessing agent-enacted influence. Synthesizing this literature, we aim to deliver: - An integrative behavioral framework that maps agent behaviors to leadership theory. - A research agenda outlining methodological standards and open questions for studying AI leadership. - Theoretical refinements that extend leadership theory to account for influence processes enacted by artificial agents. The expected outcome is a comprehensive and causally trustworthy assessment of how conversational agents perform leadership functions in psychosocial interventions, contributing both to leadership theory and to the responsible design of AI systems that increasingly shape workplace interactions.

items.title: Towards Decoding Grammar Perception: Identifying Specialized Neurons in LLMs
items.abstract: Artificial Neural Networks, the building blocks of AI, were inspired by the human brain’s network of neurons. Over the years, these networks have evolved to replicate complex capabilities of the brain, allowing them to handle tasks such as image and language processing. In the realm of Large Language Models, there has been a keen interest in making the language learning process more akin to that of humans. Motivated by neuroscience research that has shown that different grammatical categories are processed by different neurons in the brain, we show that LLMs operate in a similar way. Utilizing Llama 3 and Qwen2, we identify the most important neurons associated with the prediction of words belonging to different part-of-speech tags. Using the achieved knowledge, we train a classifier on a dataset, which shows that the activation patterns of these key neurons can reliably predict part-of-speech tags on fresh data. The results suggest that LLMs develop specialized neural representations for capturing part-of-speech tag concepts.

items.title: Towards Online Adaptive LLM-based Semantic Filtering
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) enable semantic filtering over unstructured documents using natural language predicates, but invoking an oracle LLM on every document incurs prohibitive monetary cost and online latency. Existing model-cascade approaches reduce this cost by using a lightweight proxy model to score each document and forwarding only uncertain documents to the oracle. However, their proxy models have limited generalization capability, and they typically adopt fixed sampling budgets for proxy training and threshold calibration, which insufficiently adapts to diverse online queries. To address this, we present OASIS, an online adaptive framework for LLM-based semantic filtering. OASIS combines a query-agnostic document similarity prior with query-adaptive online learning and sampling. In the offline phase, OASIS utilizes query-agnostic document similarity as a prior and constructs a document navigating spread-out graph (NSG) over document embeddings. For each online query, OASIS trains a query-conditioned graph attention network over the document NSG to obtain proxy scores through semi-supervised node classification. To allocate labels effectively, OASIS adopts density-aware active learning to explore uncertain score regions, selectively annotate informative documents, retrain the proxy, and stop early when additional labels are unlikely to improve the cascade. During threshold calibration, OASIS progressively samples an adaptively sized calibration set, adapting calibration cost to the query's score distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OASIS achieves a 1.75x-5.42x reduction in online latency and reduces the number of LLM-processed documents by 35%-75% relative to the state-of-the-art methods at an achieved accuracy of 0.9.
