items.title: Towards Operational Efficiency in Maritime Fire Response: A Collaborative Approach Using Smart Technologies and Shared Situational Awareness
items.abstract: Maritime transportation is the backbone of global trade, yet it faces significant fire safety challenges, particularly in cargo handling. Fires on container ships account for 55% of all maritime fire incidents, with 92.6% originating from cargo, often involving misdeclared dangerous goods (DG). These fires lead to catastrophic consequences, including vessel damage, container loss, and environmental pollution. The OVERHEAT EU-funded Horizon project introduces a cutting-edge Digital Solution (DS) designed to enhance operational efficiency and maritime fire safety through synchronized offshore-onshore DS enabling real-time collaboration between ship crews, port authorities, and emergency responders, providing a unified and real-time view of unfolding emergencies. The architecture leverages IoT-enabled sensors, UAV-assisted thermal imaging, and AI-powered decision support tools to detect and assess fire hazards with high accuracy and speed. This integrated awareness significantly enhances the Shared Situational Awareness (SSA) resulting in coordinated decision-making, reduced response times, which in effect improves the effectiveness of mitigation efforts. Beyond technological innovation, the OVERHEAT project also emphasizes the importance of fostering a proactive safety culture (SC). This paper presents the challenges in maritime firefighting, the design and implementation of OVERHEAT’s DS, discusses its potential for improving maritime fire safety, and outlines future validation efforts through simulation and real-world trials in European ports.

items.title: Transferable Named Sparse Features for Morphology-based Gleason Grading
items.abstract: Deep learning systems grade prostate biopsies at the level of pathologists, but most report a grade without the glandular architecture that justifies it. This work presents a grading system built on a sparse code over the tokens of a pathology foundation model. A sparse autoencoder pretrained on biopsies is aligned with multi-reader annotations, so that 69 of its 2048 features are named after Gleason morphologies such as cribriform glands, cords, and comedonecrosis. The same code feeds a grading network, which reads all features to predict Gleason patterns and the Grade Group, while morphology maps read directly from the named features. We evaluate the system on five public datasets that include needle biopsies, tissue-microarray cores, multi-reader annotations, and three scanners. The morphology maps remain stable across alignment runs and, without retraining, detect cribriform glands in external biopsies (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUROC, 0.849) and pattern 5 in unseen cores when evaluated by up to six pathologists (AUROC 0.846 to 0.919). In an independent biopsy cohort, Grade Group agreement with three pathologists on Leica scans is close to their agreement with each other. Removing the named features reduces the corresponding Gleason pattern predictions by 49% to 98%, with effects larger than those from 20 activity-matched random feature removals. These results show that a shared sparse representation can support competitive Gleason grading while providing named morphological evidence that transfers across datasets and whose contribution to grading can be measured directly.

items.title: Treatment Selection in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Conceptual Framework for Precision Therapy
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a major therapeutic challenge, with limited improvement in outcomes and substantial heterogeneity in treatment response. Systemic chemotherapy remains a cornerstone of treatment across disease stages, yet treatment selection, particularly in metastatic PDAC (mPDAC), is still driven predominantly by clinical characteristics, performance status, prior therapy, and a limited number of molecular biomarkers. The emergence of biomarker-directed therapies, including strategies targeting oncogenic KRAS alterations, demonstrates the potential of molecularly informed treatment selection but also highlights the need to identify which therapy is most likely to benefit an individual patient at a specific clinical decision point. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), multi-omics profiling, digital pathology, and prospective therapeutic trials provide an opportunity to develop comprehensive precision-treatment strategies. Existing AI approaches, including PASS-01/MULTIPL, PDACai, and CHAI, provide important foundations but remain constrained by limitations in prognostic versus predictive modeling, reliance on predominantly static or correlational representations, limited mechanistic interpretability, and incomplete integration of treatment effects and evolving tumor biology. In this narrative review, we propose a conceptual framework for individualized treatment selection in mPDAC that integrates multiscale biological and clinical data, mechanistic graph-based pathway representations, multimodal transformer models, and causal estimation of individualized treatment effects. This framework shifts AI-enabled precision oncology from static biomarker prediction toward mechanistically informed, uncertainty-aware, causally grounded treatment selection, with the potential to adapt as tumor biology, therapeutic options, and clinical evidence evolve. Although initially focused on mPDAC, the framework provides a generalizable architecture for individualized treatment selection across other biologically heterogeneous cancers.

items.title: TRIANGULATE: Trust-minimized MRV for AI normative audits — multimodal triangulation so the answer does not depend on trusting any single measurer
items.abstract: Measurement–reporting–verification (MRV) is load-bearing wherever claimed contribution must be checked against real contribution — in carbon markets, in the verified-contribution accounting proposed for life-capacity economies, and in audits that classify what objective an AI system appears to pursue. Yet every MRV pipeline rests on a measurer, and a measurer is a trust dependency. The physical world solved a structurally identical problem decades ago: no single satellite, sensor tower, or field plot is trusted to estimate carbon stock; heterogeneous modalities with different bias profiles are triangulated, and disagreement between them is information, not noise. We instantiate the same pattern for AI normative audits. Our pipeline combines three measurement modalities — LLM judge families (remote, scalable, biased), a human gold set (local, expensive, ground-truth), and revealed-preference behavioral tasks — behind preregistered gates that can fail and be reported, a scorer-of-record selected by coded-seed agreement, and a published rejected-instrument exhibit. Applied to a 4,164-record audit of open-weight model objectives, the system localizes exactly which judgment is contested: judge–human agreement is Cohen's κ=0.22 overall, but failure concentrates on the boundary question ("does this text presume an objective at all," κ≈0.19) while direction survives (φ-share 29.8% human vs 25.5% judge on the jointly objective-bearing subset). We therefore report magnitudes as judge-family quantities and direction as a cross-modal finding — decomposition reporting that binds each claim to the level its weakest instrument supports. Part of the LESS–IS–MORE program.

items.title: Trust and calibrated professional reliance in construction AI: a cross-national study of professional judgement
items.abstract: Trust remains insufficiently understood in construction AI, particularly where AI outputs inform safety-critical or contractual decisions with professional and legal consequences. This study investigates how construction professionals evaluate and justify trust under technical uncertainty, site variability and professional accountability. A cross-national mixed-methods design was used to analyse 1,233 valid survey responses from professionals in managerial, technical, design and site-based roles across Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States. The study distinguishes trust calibration, defined as aligning trust with an AI system’s capabilities and limitations, from calibrated professional reliance, whereby AI outputs are relied upon only when they are technically reliable, contextually appropriate and professionally defensible. Across the three countries, accuracy, reliability and contextual alignment formed the basis for reliance, while governance, explainability, transparency and accountability supported reliance under safety, contractual and regulatory scrutiny. The main risks concerned unreliable predictions and data privacy and security, while the main benefits were efficiency, planning accuracy and decision support. The study advances trust-in-AI research by conceptualizing calibrated professional reliance as a construction-specific judgement shaped by technical performance, contextual fit and professional accountability. These findings explain how construction professionals decide whether to accept, verify, modify, override or reject AI outputs.

items.title: Trust and Verification in Digital Impersonation and Cyber Deception: A Human Factors Review and Research Agenda
items.abstract: Digital impersonation exploits trust, verification behavior, and decision-making under uncertainty. This structured narrative review synthesizes selected literature on cybersecurity, social engineering, trust in automation, AI-mediated communication, and synthetic media. Four themes organize the analysis: trust calibration, cognitive biases and social influence, verification failure, and human-centered defenses. The literature suggests that susceptibility reflects interactions among credibility cues, authority pressure, urgency, cognitive demands, and organizational practices. Generative AI can reproduce familiar communication cues, challenging verification based on appearance, fluency, or sensory familiarity. However, evidence from conventional phishing and automation research does not establish the magnitude of these effects in every AI-enabled setting. The review proposes research priorities addressing trust measurement, verification fatigue, organizational culture, and interactive deception. Its central implication is that effective defense requires usable verification procedures and organizational support alongside technical detection and training.

items.title: Tuning Cu/diamond interfacial thermal conductance via nitrogen-termination engineering
items.abstract: Cu-diamond composites are recognized as promising high-thermal-conductivity candidates for electronic cooling, offering tunable properties and competitive cost. However, their performance is significantly limited by the poor Cu/diamond interfacial thermal conductance (ITC). Here, we propose a nitrogen-termination strategy to tune the ITC of Cu/diamond interfaces and unravel atomistic mechanisms by which nitride interlayers tailor phonon transport. Based on the MACE machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) framework, we fine-tune the pre-trained MACE-MPA-0 foundation model by incorporating customized C-N-Cu training datasets. Incorporating non-equilibrium molecular dynamics with MLIP-driven lattice dynamics simulations, we demonstrate that anharmonic effects contribute ∼60% to the ITC, and simply introducing N-termination on the diamond surface enhances the ITC by 10% compared to the bare Cu/diamond interface. However, the enhancement of harmonic phonon transmission contributes ∼80% of the ITC improvement. Mode-resolved phonon spectroscopy reveals that the LA phonons with frequencies above 4 THz and wavevectors near the Γ-X and Γ-U directions are selectively modulated by N-termination engineering. Analyses of local vibrational states and interfacial bonding further indicate that the N-termination on diamond tunes the interfacial heat conduction via surficial mass modification and chemical bonding regulation, as evidenced by variations in LDOS overlaps and COHP spectra. These findings open venues for tuning heat transfer across Cu/diamond interfaces via non-metallic modification-which avoids the graphitization issues associated with metallic coatings-and provide novel guidelines for upgrading the phonon-mediated heat transfer in Cu-diamond composites.

items.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) seeks to identify emotions conveyed through or elicited by media comprising diverse modality compositions. Research in this field has largely evolved along two paradigms: task-specific models and approaches based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Despite their distinct strengths, neither fully reconciles three capabilities essential to human-like emotion understanding: cross-task generalization, efficient decision-making, and receptiveness to multiple plausible interpretations. Inspired by recent advances in decision models, we explore a unified framework that maps multimodal inputs, guided by natural language instructions, directly to distributions over candidate options, addressing these requirements through direct probabilistic decisions. We instantiate this framework in UEmo-D1, the first decision model for MER to our knowledge. To support joint training and systematic evaluation, we also curate UEmo-Data, comprising 977,270 training samples and 41 evaluation subsets across six MER tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate UEmo-D1's combination of strong recognition performance, low inference latency, and well-calibrated confidence estimates. Complementary analyses further reveal how training strategies and data composition influence these capabilities, providing practical insights into unified MER modeling. Together, our findings establish decision models as a feasible direction toward human-level emotion recognition. Project page: https://github.com/wdqqdw/UEmo-D1.

items.title: Understanding university students’ AI usage decisions in Vietnam
items.abstract: This study examines the factors associated with university students’ decisions to use artificial intelligence (AI) in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, drawing on an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Data were collected from 369 students across 40 universities, including 53 international students (14.36%), and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The findings support all seven hypothesized direct relationships. Facilitating conditions are positively associated with perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, while perceived ease of use is positively related to perceived usefulness and intention to use. Perceived usefulness shows the strongest direct association with behavioral intention (β = 0.534), whereas intention to use is the strongest direct predictor of self-reported AI usage decisions (β = 0.480). Significant indirect effects further highlight the interconnected roles of technological perceptions and behavioral intention. The study contributes to technology acceptance research by examining reported AI usage decisions alongside behavioral intention within a higher education setting involving students from different national backgrounds. The findings suggest that universities, instructors, and student support services should strengthen access to AI tools, provide responsible-use guidance, and consider multilingual academic support. Because the analysis uses pooled, cross-sectional data, the findings do not establish causal relationships or international student-specific effects.

items.title: Usability of an artificial intelligence enabled Participation and Environment Measure prototype for family-centered goal setting support in pediatric rehabilitation
items.abstract: Family-centered care coordination (FC-CC) in pediatric rehabilitation benefits from tools that support caregivers in contributing to personalized service planning for their children. Participation and Environment Measure (PEM) is a digital application that is being further developed to support FC-CC in early intervention (EI). PEM is being further developed to include the Young Children’s Participation and Environment Measure (YC-PEM) electronic patient-reported outcome and a companion PEM-Plus (PEM+) goal setting intervention. This study examined usability of the first artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled PEM prototype. Caregivers from an urban EI program met these eligibility criteria: (1) were at least 18 years old; (2) identified as the parent or legal guardian of a child enrolled in EI services; (3) read, wrote, and spoke English; (4) had internet and telephone access; and (5) had a child 0–3 years old who received EI services for 3 or more months. Participants completed the AI-enabled PEM application with access to a debiased prototypic conversational agent. PEM usability was assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS), and chatbot usability was assessed along four BOT Usability Scale (BUS-11) domains: 1) accessibility of chatbot functions; 2) functional interactive conversation; 3) privacy and security; and 4) timely response. Univariate logistic regression models were used to examine associations between each of the four BUS-11 domains and PEM+ engagement. Eleven female caregivers of children (mean age: 24.5 months) enrolled, 66.7% of whom interacted with the prototypic chatbot during one or more iterations of the PEM+ intervention. Overall PEM usability remained acceptable. While overall chatbot usability was very poor (Mdn = 53.4%, IQR = 50.0, 55.4), caregiver perceptions of chatbot usability were average for accessibility of chatbot functions (Mdn = 3.8, IQR = 3.0, 4.0) and good for privacy and security ( M = 3.1, Range = 2.0–5.0). Higher caregiver perceptions of chatbot usability did not significantly increase odds of PEM+ intervention use. Findings indicate that an AI-enabled PEM retains adequate usability. A chatbot integrated within the PEM+ intervention is accessible and secure, though its functional interactive conversation and timely responses could benefit from further development to increase odds of its use in an EI service context. items.title: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence by Production Engineering Students at the Federal University of Amazonas in the First Semester of 2026
items.abstract: This study analyzed Production Engineering students’ use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) at FT/UFAM, Brazil, in the first semester of 2026 to support pedagogical decisions. This exploratory, descriptive, and quantitative study surveyed 106 of the 263 enrolled students through non-probability convenience sampling. Course- level responses were screened with consistency rules based on institutional documents and analyzed using descriptive statistics, a chi-square test, and generalized estimating equations. In all, 87.7% of respondents use GenAI, mainly ChatGPT and Gemini, to improve their writing and solve problems. Differences between semester blocks varied across data-screening scenarios, which precludes conclusions about a pattern of use throughout the program. Among users, 63% learned to use these tools on their own and only 16% from university instructors; 68% reported difficulties with GenAI literacy and 61% a lack of clear guidelines. Among respondents, widespread GenAI adoption contrasts with the limited role of instructors as a reported source of learning and with the absence of program- specific guidelines: the central challenge is not to introduce GenAI but to provide pedagogical guidance for a practice that is already widespread. We recommend combining AI literacy, explicit rules in course syllabi, and assessments that value the learning process and transparency of use.

items.title: Usefulness of an Exoscope-assisted Head-mounted Display for Neurosurgical Assistants in En Bloc Resection of Malignant Skull Base Tumors: A 2-case Report
items.abstract: Exoscopic neurosurgery has become increasingly widespread; however, limitations associated with large external monitors remain, particularly in complex multidisciplinary procedures. To address these issues, we introduced a head-mounted display during exoscopic surgery and evaluated its usefulness from the assistant's perspective in 2 cases. The first case involved a man in his 60s with an intraorbital malignant solitary fibrous tumor who underwent left orbital exenteration for en bloc tumor resection. The second case involved a woman in her 40s with a progressively enlarging intraorbital liposarcoma who underwent the same procedure. In both cases, surgery was performed simultaneously by 2 teams: an endoscopic endonasal approach by the otolaryngology–head and neck surgery team and a transcranial approach by the neurosurgical team. An exoscope (ORBEYE; Olympus, Tokyo, Japan) and head-mounted display (Weaps; Hogy Medical, Tokyo, Japan) were used for visualization, and the duration of head-mounted display use exceeded 2 hours in each case. The head-mounted display enabled the assistant to participate while maintaining an ergonomic upright posture without the need to turn toward an external monitor. Continuous high-resolution visualization directly in front of the eyes facilitated effective assistance, improved understanding of surgical anatomy and workflow, and allowed stable participation throughout the procedure, even in a crowded operative environment. The combined use of a head-mounted display with an exoscope may provide an improved visualization environment for surgical assistants and represents a promising approach to overcome limitations of conventional monitor-based exoscopic surgery.

items.title: Using generative AI to support qualitative coding of reflections on inclusion by students in Swedish special education programmes
items.abstract: This exploratory study examined the possibilities and limitations of using generative AI as a supplementary tool for qualitative coding of written reflections produced by students in Swedish special education programmes. The empirical material comprised 99 responses to a debate article on inclusion and special educational perspectives. A theory-informed coding framework distinguished compensatory, relational and dilemma perspectives as non-exhaustive, potentially overlapping ideal types in naturally occurring texts. Two human raters independently coded a stratified random subsample of 20 texts, with ChatGPT as an additional coder using a specified prompting procedure. Human–human agreement was 80% (Cohen’s kappa = 0.70); agreement between each human rater and ChatGPT was 65% (kappa = 0.46 and 0.42). Under the tested configuration, ChatGPT identified no compensatory cases and tended to interpret peripheral forms of inclusion as dilemma-oriented. A post hoc prompt refinement, informed by errors in the same subsample and applied only to six compensatory cases, changed several outputs but provided no independent test of improved performance. Findings therefore concern this model-prompt-data configuration rather than large language models’ inherent capabilities. Agreement, systematic disagreement and prompt sensitivity can inform methodological reflection, underscoring the need for transparent procedures, held-out validation and human interpretive judgement in normatively complex qualitative analysis.

items.title: Using instruction-based LLMs for psychological Big Five personality measurement
items.abstract: This datasets are part of master thesis in psychology that examines how Artificial Intelligence (AI)—specifically instruction based Large Language Models (LLMs)—can serve as psychological measurement tools for personality analysis. The goal was to assess whether LLMs can identify Big Five personality traits from texts written by historical figures. A custom AI-based instrument was developed and validated using the Pennebaker and King (1999) Essays dataset, then applied to works by Virginia Woolf, George Orwell, and Walter Benjamin. Results indicate that LLMs can generate consistent and theoretically plausible personality profiles.

items.title: Using without understanding: AI literacy and trust in large language models among elementary school children in Germany
items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly shape children’s learning, fostering informed and critical engagement has become an urgent educational task. This study examines children’s AI literacy and trust in LLMs during a learning interaction. Thirty children aged 8-10 years participated in semi-structured interviews combined with an interaction task using a customized LLM. Children used the system competently, yet their conceptual understanding remained fragmented. At the same time, children placed high trust in the LLM’s ability and benevolence, while perceptions of integrity, particularly regarding data privacy, were more cautious. Their reasoning was frequently anthropomorphic, reinforced by social cues such as natural language use and emojis. The human analogy, however, was applied selectively. Children explained the system’s errors through human fallibility, but most considered algorithmic bias impossible, treating prejudice as a uniquely human trait. These findings suggest that AI literacy education should begin in elementary school and explicitly address questions of fairness, building on children’s intuition that AI learns from humans.

items.title: Virtual Reality (VR)-Based Safety Training for Post-Disaster Responders and Workers: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Post-disaster responders and workers operate in hazardous environments that require rapid decision-making, hazard recognition, and effective safety training. Virtual reality (VR) has emerged in recent years as an innovative tool for immersive occupational safety and health education. This scoping review systematically examines peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 on the use of VR for safety training among personnel across a broad range of fields and populations who perform or are trained to perform disaster and emergency response functions. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, five electronic databases (PubMed, ProQuest Central, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and ERIC) were searched, resulting in 2202 identified articles; 19 of which met the inclusion criteria after screening and eligibility assessments. The reviewed studies suggest that VR-based safety training, which uses fully immersive simulated environments, can improve learner engagement, situational awareness, hazard recognition, decision-making, and confidence in disaster response scenarios. Several studies have reported higher user satisfaction and increased realism compared with traditional instructional methods such as classroom-based instruction or mock drills. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous, with limitations including small sample sizes, technical challenges, limited scenario diversity, and insufficient long-term evaluation of training outcomes. Overall, VR is a promising supplement to traditional safety and health training for post-disaster responders and workers; however, additional longitudinal research and large-scale studies are needed to further evaluate its effectiveness and long-term applicability in various disaster-response settings.

items.title: VisAlloc: Allocating Visual Supervision for On-Policy Self-Distillation
items.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising approach to improving visual reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, not all samples benefit equally from privileged visual guidance, and uniform token supervision can dilute visually grounded signals. We propose VisAlloc, a dual-level framework combining sample-level visual filtering with token-level counterfactual reweighting. A fixed paired-teacher filter retains samples answered correctly from an evidence-centered positive crop but incorrectly from a spatially displaced negative crop. At the token level, both EMA teachers score the same student-generated response, and their absolute log-probability differences measure view sensitivity. Additional supervision targets tokens admitted by sensitivity or teacher-distribution disagreement, with shared frozen-prior, template-bigram, and student--teacher divergence gates. Inverse-frequency redistribution preserves the total additional weight within each micro-batch, while the positive teacher remains the sole distillation target. Inference requires only the full-image student. Across eight benchmarks, our 4B and 9B models achieve macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, outperforming Vision-OPD reproductions by 0.97 and 0.52 points, respectively. items.title: Vision-driven retrieval-augmented decision support for plant disease diagnosis using EfficientNetV2 and large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Accurate and timely plant disease diagnosis is essential for sustainable agricultural production and precision farming. However, most existing agricultural decision support systems treat visual disease diagnosis and agronomic recommendation generation as separate processes, either providing image classification results alone or generating recommendations with large language models that are not grounded in domain-specific knowledge. To address this limitation, this study introduces EffiToRag, an end-to-end decision support framework that integrates an EfficientNetV2-based visual diagnosis module with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Rather than relying solely on free-text queries for disease-level retrieval, the proposed approach uses the disease class predicted by EfficientNetV2 as the primary key for retrieving the corresponding record from a structured agronomic knowledge base constructed from peer-reviewed scientific publications and official phytopathological guidelines. The visual diagnosis module was trained using Progressive Training and Class-Aware Tiered Augmentation (CATA) to account for differences in class representation. On a held-out test set comprising 11,621 images across 60 plant health classes, EfficientNetV2-M achieved 99.13% accuracy and a Macro F1 score of 0.9889, with an inference time of 4.39 ms per image on the evaluated GPU. For 500 user queries, the system selected query-relevant knowledge fields with a precision of 0.972 and a recall of 0.985. The factual-consistency assessment combined GPT-4-based evaluation and manual expert review of a random sample of 100 diagnostic reports and yielded a mean factual-consistency score of 0.99. The experts also assigned these reports a mean applicability score of 4.85/5.0. These findings show that visual disease classification, structured agronomic knowledge retrieval, and LLM-based recommendation generation can be integrated within a single decision support pipeline for precision agriculture.

items.title: VOL-Agent: Programming Your Film via Video Orchestration Language Agentic System
items.abstract: Recent video foundation models generate high-quality and limited-length clips, but orchestrating them into minute-level, story-coherent films remains an open problem. Existing video agents highly rely on natural-language planning or predefined workflows, which make their production hard to program, customize, and extend. Therefore, we introduce VOL-Agent, a programmable video agent built on a Video Orchestration Language (VOL). With static compilation and verification, followed by runtime dynamic loading, VOL-Agent decouples structural reliability from execution flexibility. Through the skill-driven executor, VOL-Agent dynamically resolves tools and skills from an open-world repository and supports user-defined skills in natural language. Moreover, VOL-Agent is capable of crafting new director skills from learned knowledge and improves itself through feedback to accumulate filmmaking knowledge. To overcome the disconnect between different segments, we apply a structural memory mechanism to record and recall world and entity states, sustaining entity and scene consistency across different shots. Critic feedback supports local revision, while reusable filmmaking knowledge and experiences can be retained for subsequent tasks. Experiments on three benchmarks show that VOL-Agent generates minute-scale videos with strong overall quality and limited cost.

items.title: Weighing the Envelope: Component Weight and Arbitration in Envelope-Layer Defenses for a Single LLM Agent
items.abstract: The envelope layer is the channel through which malicious content enters an LLM agent. Prior work established label and memory effects on multi-agent A2A envelopes, but the weight structure when MCP tools and memory coexist in a single agent remains unclear. Our threat model assumes an attacker pre-plants a malicious tool and poisons long-term memory; a benign user request inadvertently triggers it, and the attacker never enters the conversation. Following GDA Measurement and A/B/C/D, we measure how labels, memory, tool roles, and the backend shape invocation decisions across label-memory conflict, tool roles, robustness, and tool generalization. A tool-side forced-verification label substantially reduces semantic breach, but strong success memory pulls it back; a memory-side downgrade statement returns the outcome to the level of the label alone. The label works through mandatory implementation inspection plus default denial, not length or format; memory authorization wording erodes it with dose, while position and multi-turn pressure do not change the defense direction. Tool roles divide label effects into substitution, suppression, and boundary failure: low penetration is not safety, local leakage is the main residual risk, and a second malicious tool shows the same direction. Envelope labels are not a switch but a measurable, reversible weight constrained by backend and tool role, acting as a soft gate and risk signal within a broader defense rather than a substitute for permissions, sandboxing, or human review.

items.title: Werkstattbericht: Erfahrungen aus der Zusammenarbeit mit KI-Agenten
items.abstract: This practice-based and philosophical paper reflects on human collaboration with AI agents, especially for learning expert-level skills in higher education. Using the development of the AI-supported multi-agent system LASSI as an example, it narrates a learning journey in three phases: productive amazement, a shift in authorship, and finally taking responsibility. Perspectives of a developer, a professor, and students show how human-agent systems change through collaboration. Three philosophical dimensions – embodied knowledge, enhanced technologies, and embedded ethics – are used to assess potentials and risks: what happens when intelligence is disembodied, human capabilities are outsourced to technology, and values are encoded? The paper argues that agents should not be treated as neutral tools but as co-shapers within the sociotechnical system of education. It concludes by portraying universities as thinking workshops that must redefine their role with AI: away from exam-driven routines toward cultivating judgment and self-reflection.

items.title: What Does Generalizable AI in Drug Discovery Really Mean?
items.abstract: Abstract Machine learning models increasingly contribute to drug discovery, but their utility depends on performing reliably in their intended deployment setting. Although model generalization is invoked frequently, the drug discovery community lacks a shared vocabulary for how models actually achieve transferability beyond their training data. We argue that achieving generalization requires examining how a model’s inductive bias interacts with its training data to shape the notion of similarity it learns. Without a bias that makes relevant recurring relationships easier to learn as opposed to incidental correlations, models exploit dataset-specific shortcuts. These shortcuts yield high benchmark performance but fail in prospective applications. We therefore propose evaluation principles tailored to a model’s architecture, using diagnostic controls and train−test splits that distinguish transferable learning from the retrieval of familiar training data. This Perspective shows how representational choices shape failure modes across pose-dependent, pose-independent, and foundation model paradigms, and provides a practical framework to help researchers expose shortcuts and interpret predictions.

items.title: What is Hybrid Intelligence? Toward a Multi-Layered Model for Complex Problem-Solving
items.abstract: The dominant automation paradigm, which measures artificial intelligence by its capacity to act independently of humans, is increasingly inadequate for complex problem-solving. This article develops the concept of Hybrid Intelligence, defined as an adaptive, self-regulating system arising from the synergistic integration of human and artificial intelligence to enhance cognitive abilities. Revisiting the cognitive-tools tradition through an information-processing lens, it argues that generative AI dissolves the safeguard that once ensured tools amplified rather than supplanted human thinking. It then specifies a layered, multi-agentic architecture in which AI agents and agentic AI are embedded within contextual and collaborative human layers. It applies this architecture to the phases of complex problem-solving. The overriding argument is that sustainable Hybrid Intelligence requires enduring theoretical foundations that outlast individual model releases, ensuring that human–AI collaboration genuinely enhances, rather than inadvertently constrains, human cognitive agency.

items.title: What Majority Labels Hide: Annotator Disagreement and Model Errors in Multi-Dialect Arabic Sexism Detection
items.abstract: Judgements of sexism are subjective and may vary across communities, yet sexism detection datasets usually reduce annotator judgements to a single majority label, obscuring disagreement and how models behave on contested cases. We introduce MuDAS, a dataset of YouTube comments in Saudi, Egyptian and Moroccan Arabic, each labelled by three native speakers of its dialect, with the individual annotations preserved. We use it to evaluate Arabic encoders fine-tuned with hard-label, soft-label and perspectivist objectives, GPT-5.6 Terra, and four Arabic-centric large language models. Model errors are more frequent on comments with annotator disagreement. Despite relatively close Macro-F1 scores, GPT-5.6 Terra and the fine-tuned encoders exhibit contrasting error patterns: GPT-5.6 Terra, even with the annotators' definition of sexism, over-classifies gender-related content such as religious advice on modesty, whereas the encoders miss implicit and prescriptive sexism. The Arabic-centric models also over-predict sexism and remain below the encoders. Disagreement-aware learning preserves Macro-F1, but soft labels improve alignment with annotators on contested comments at the expense of unanimous ones, and neither paradigm reliably identifies contested comments. Lower performance on Egyptian Arabic, clearest for the large language models, is not fully explained by the examined measures of test-set composition and dialectness. Majority-label scores can therefore hide contrasting error patterns that matter for content moderation.

items.title: What Were You Thinking? An LLM-Driven Large-Scale Study of Refactoring Motivations in Open Source Projects
items.abstract: Context . Code refactoring improves software quality without changing external behavior. Despite its advantages, its benefits are hindered by the considerable cost of time, resources, and continuous effort it demands. Aim . Understanding why developers refactor, and which metrics capture these motivations, may support wider and more effective use of refactoring in practice. Method . We performed a large-scale empirical study to analyze developers’ refactoring activity, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify underlying motivations from version control data, comparing our findings with previous motivations reported in the literature. Results . LLMs matched human judgment in 80% of cases, but aligned with literature-based motivations in only 47%. They enriched 22% of motivations with more detailed rationale, often highlighting readability, clarity, and structural improvements. Most motivations were pragmatic, focused on simplification and maintainability. While metrics related to developer experience and code readability ranked highest, their correlation with motivation categories was weak. Conclusions . We conclude that LLMs effectively capture surface-level motivations but struggle with architectural reasoning. Their value lies in providing localized explanations, which, when combined with software metrics, can form hybrid approaches. Such integration offers a promising path toward prioritizing refactoring more systematically and balancing short-term improvements with long-term architectural goals.

items.title: When "brain outsourcing" becomes habit: governmentality dilemmas and learning alienation in agentic workflows
items.abstract: The spread of generative AI has made "brain outsourcing"—delegating cognitive tasks to AI—a common phenomenon in higher education, especially in low-tier private undergraduate colleges. Existing studies explain it mainly at the individual level, neglecting the institutional consequences of the technologies used to govern it. Drawing on design-based research principles, this study conducted a three-group quasi-experiment in a Data Structures course at such a college: an adversarial workflow (Group A, n = 36), a negotiative workflow (Group B, n = 40), and a traditional control group (n = 44), triangulated across five chains of evidence. Results show that Group A's direct-dumping rate fell to 11.1% (vs. 57.5% and 75.0%), yet concealed forms—cosmetic modification and division-of-labor outsourcing—rose compensatorily, leaving the composite outsourcing index unchanged across groups (p = 0.864). Process engagement rose sharply while output authenticity stayed low (comment–code matching 3.62/5; only 27.8% of difficulty tags authentic), indicating "performative engagement". Only 1 of 120 students adopted a self-regulated strategy. In Group A, perceived control rose (+2.17) and negotiation space fell (−0.91) without meaningful growth in autonomy; the 18.3-point advantage over the control group in comprehension depth shrank to 6.8 points in transfer application. The "non-outsourceable" workflow thus changed outsourcing's form, not its deep structure, alienating learning into an adversarial game of evading detection—a new hidden curriculum. Agent design should shift from adversarial surveillance to dialogic support.
